evidence.claim: The Wyoming Office of Tourism describes a 25-mile historic route centered on western migration, with a former campsite and surviving charcoal kilns.
evidence.quote: Twenty-five miles of back roads will lead you from a real western ghost town to Muddy Creek, one of the most famous camping spots of the western migration.

evidence.quote: Go south on WY-173 to the ghost town of Piedmont. Then return north on WY-173 to I-80 at exit 24, known as the LeRoy exit.

evidence.claim: Water and tall bunchgrass made Muddy Creek a campsite for westward travelers and their animals.

evidence.claim: The transcontinental railroad passed through in 1869.

evidence.claim: At Piedmont, helper engines needed wood and water to work a steep railroad grade, bringing railroad families into town.

evidence.claim: Later, the Aspen tunnel eliminated that winding climb; the new line bypassed Piedmont by several miles, and the town declined.

flags: The archived brochure files 01 and 07 contain only a Wayback Machine wrapper. Gravel surface, adverse-weather suitability and private ownership of Piedmont in the current draft lack usable cache support and were dropped.

The tourism page identifies a historic backway but does not establish a formal designation date or road-construction history. Road character beyond back roads is undocumented; overview follows the transport corridor's history.

Driving order reverses the current draft to follow strip miles from Piedmont toward Fort Bridger. The tourism page supports the branched route; it does not supply a precise Muddy Creek stop coordinate.
Kiln dates conflict: Piedmont article gives 1877; kiln article gives 1869. Omitted construction year and questionable circumference figure.
Fort Bridger article gives both 1842 and 1843 for establishment; omitted the date.
Current draft's claim that the road ends at Piedmont contradicts the tourism description of a return branch to I-80; corrected.
Muddy Creek moment is shorter than 90 words because additional campsite anecdotes would not strengthen the story.
Overview and simple moments remain short: road surface and road-building history are absent, while unresolved kiln and fort dates limit useful historical detail.
